effect_estimate.comment: Appended table/figure pages (PDF pp. 39-46, 48, 50) are blank in the PDF text extract, so all point estimates and test descriptions are extracted strictly from the main text and footnotes. No exact 95% CIs or exact p-values are printed in the prose, though significance thresholds (10% and 5% levels), first-stage partial F-statistics, and one LIML standard error are stated.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive disparities: In 1980, 61% of small houses (1-2 rooms, proxy for migrant/informal housing) vs. 86% of large houses (6-7 rooms) had a central water connection, and 17% vs. 54% had full service (electricity, central water, and central sewer); in 1991, unweighted central water coverage was 57% for small houses (1-3 rooms) vs. 89% for large houses (7-9 rooms), while 14% of urban households overall lacked central water and 51% lacked full service. Strategic determinants of 1991 small-house central water provision (urban-area fixed effects): opponent localities' weighted small-house water servicing had a negative strategic reaction slope of beta = -0.43 in lagged-1980 OLS and beta = -0.53 in spatial MLE (-0.69 OLS and -0.59 MLE with equal weights), implying ~0.45 percentage points lower own small-house water servicing per 1 percentage-point opponent increase; rich-and-large localities exhibited strategic under-servicing via a negative income-by-size interaction (moving from lowest to highest income and size quintiles raised servicing by 0.48 ignoring interaction, reduced by 0.16 in the top income/size quintile interaction; in 23 two- or three-locality urban areas, marginal income effects turned negative above 0.5 SD above mean size and marginal size effects turned negative above 1 SD above mean income), with null effects in counterfactuals for 1991 large houses and post-democratization 2000 small houses. Effect of 1991 small-house water servicing on 1991-2000 locality household growth (IV with geology/insolation and 1970 historical instruments, urban-area FE): 2SLS coefficient = 0.74 (0.77 with shorter instrument list; 0.78 with river/altitude instruments; p < 0.10, first-stage partial F ~ 13; LIML significant at just over the 5% level), meaning at a point estimate of 0.8 a 1 SD (0.21) increase in servicing raised decadal household growth by 0.17 (mean growth = 0.40), while a 1 SD servicing reduction lowered 1991-2000 low-educated household growth by 0.17 (2SLS, statistically significant) and similarly reduced higher-educated household growth (p ~ 0.05); using central water share among untitled homes gave OLS = -0.16 and LIML = 1.82 (SE = 2.22, first-stage F = 6.2). In 1980 district-FE rent hedonics, central water commanded a 12% rent premium in Sao Paulo and 23% in Rio de Janeiro, and central sewer commanded 9% and 18%, respectively.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Assigned 1 (documented association). Although ROBINS-I applies because Section 5 uses IV (2SLS/LIML) to estimate how 1991 small-house water servicing affects subsequent population growth, overall ROBINS-I risk of bias is Serious (modest first-stage F ~ 13 with multiple endogenous regressors, potential geological exclusion-restriction violations via private water costs noted by authors on pp. 30 and 33, weak IV F = 6.2 for untitled housing, and non-IV lagged-OLS/spatial-MLE estimation in Section 4 where water provision is the outcome). Moreover, municipal connection denials and pre-1988 statutory prohibitions are not directly observed administratively; instead, strategic exclusion is inferred from statistical associations across census house-size/tenure water-connection shares, municipal lot-size zoning cross-tabulations, and spatial reaction regressions.

mechanism_flags.comment: Paper examines pre-1988 statutory illegality of servicing untitled favelas and zoning-noncompliant loteamentos, national (125 m2) and stricter local minimum lot-size zoning laws, lack of formal land title, strategic local discretion in under-provisioning central water to small/informal houses, metropolitan fragmentation across competing municipios (and municipal water vs. state sewer authority), and inter-locality strategic competition and local electoral preferences.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Non-randomized quasi-experimental / observational econometric policy study employing instrumental variables (2SLS and LIML) with urban-area fixed effects in Section 5 to evaluate the causal impact of locality water-servicing policy, alongside lagged-covariate OLS and spatial autoregressive MLE models with urban-area fixed effects in Section 4. Matches ROBINS-I per RISK_OF_BIAS.md Section 1.

sample_size.comment: Full dataset covers 447 MCAs (659 municipalities in 1991) in 123 urban areas across the 1970, 1980, 1991, and 2000 censuses (plus 1999/2005 IBGE municipal regulatory censuses). Main econometric specifications restrict to 351 predominantly urban MCAs (>=50% urban in 1991) in 55 multi-MCA urban areas (326 MCAs in robustness checks dropping 25 MCAs without a >=65% dominant municipality). Descriptive tables also report 429 urbanized localities in 1991 and a constant panel of 258 localities >=50% urbanized in 1970; non-linear strategic-interaction models use 23 two- or three-locality urban areas (59 localities: 10 two-locality and 13 three-locality urban areas); Appendix A rent hedonics cover rental units across 56 districts in Sao Paulo and 24 districts in Rio de Janeiro in 1980 (exact N of rental units in Table A1 is on blank table page PDF p. 48).
sample_size.value: 447 localities (Minimum Comparable Areas, comprising 659 municipalities in 1991) across 123 urban areas overall (1970, 1980, 1991, and 2000 Brazilian Population Censuses); main regression sample of 351 urban localities (MCAs) in 55 multi-locality urban areas; constant urbanized panel of 258 localities (1970-2000); restricted strategic-interaction subsample of 59 localities in 23 two- or three-locality urban areas

study_design.comment: Combines (1) spatial strategic-interaction regressions (OLS with 1980 lagged covariates and spatial autoregressive/error MLE with urban-area fixed effects) modeling 1991 locality central water provision to small houses, (2) quasi-experimental instrumental-variables regressions (2SLS and LIML with urban-area fixed effects, using porous geology/insolation and 1970 historical instruments) estimating effects of 1991 water servicing on 1991-2000 locality household growth and educational composition, and (3) 1980 district-fixed-effects hedonic rent regressions in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.
study_design.value: Observational spatial-econometric (lagged-covariate OLS and spatial MLE) and quasi-experimental instrumental-variables (2SLS and LIML) panel/cross-sectional study of urban localities with urban-area fixed effects
